webpage.text:
Xbox 360 sales hit 30 million | Technology

We know how much you love stat stories... Yes, today Microsoft announced that sales of its Xbox 360 console have passed the 30 million mark, with the Xbox Live community hitting an impressive 20 million people in 26 countries - which means it's now in more homes than any satellite television provider, points out the excited press release. Here are some more Xbox-o-facts:

> Over the course of this console generation, U.S. consumers alone have spent $14.5 billion across all categories on Xbox 360 at retail. [...] To date, consumers have downloaded nearly 1 billion pieces of gaming and entertainment content from Xbox LIVE Marketplace, including a broad array of premium high- and standard-definition movies and TV shows from top studios and networks around the world.
> 
> In addition, Xbox 360 continues to be the platform of choice for the industry's top games, generating $5.9 billion in sales to date at U.S. retail for third-party publishers, which is more than those of current-generation consoles combined. Xbox 360 also leads current-generation consoles in game purchases, with consumers owning an average of 8.3 titles each.

So as things stand, Xbox 360 is still 20 million units behind Wii, but stands eight million ahead of PS3. The games-per-user figure is impressive, though - I'd be surprised if the Wii average is even half of that. I don't really have anything else to write on this matter. But stats are great, though aren't they?

Tech Focus: Next-Gen Consoles vs. The Age of Austerity

Digital Foundry on how the console platform holders are factoring in the new economic era into their designs


As all eyes turn to the next generation in gaming hardware, expectations on the level of processing power we look forward to should perhaps be tempered. Call it austerity, call it simply living within your means, the fact is that it's not just governments and families that are counting the pennies - it's the console platform holders too.

In many ways, the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 are very much products of their era. Back in 2005 there was a sense of economic invincibility in the air - and this very much permeates the design of both the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3. Let's take a look at the Microsoft console to start with: originally specced with just 256MB of RAM, it took an impassioned plea from Epic Games to see the console's memory spec doubled to its current 512MB - a move that Mark Rein reckons cost Microsoft a "hefty ransom" Doctor Evil would be proud of: one billion dollars.

> "Xbox 360 and PS3 were products of an era of economic invincibility - their next-gen replacements will be built very much with cost in mind"

"We really wanted a hard drive in every single machine; that was something we really wanted but we realised that the 512 megs of RAM was way more important," Rein said in a Major Nelson podcast. "Otherwise you couldn't do this level of graphics if you had to both write your program and do your graphics in 256 megs. Nothing would really look that HD."

The story continues with an exchange that, taken at face value, perhaps helped define the quality standards of the current console generation - while at the same time revealing how desperate Microsoft was to challenge Sony's supremacy in the marketplace.

"So we argued, and argued, and what Tim [Sweeney] did is... he actually sent a screenshot of what Gears of War would look like if we only had 256 megs of memory. So the day they made the decision, we were apparently the first developer they called... we were at Game Developers Conference, was it two years ago, and then I got a call from the chief financial officer of MGS and he said 'I just want you to know you cost me a billion dollars' and I said, 'we did a favour for a billion gamers'."

Leaving aside the woeful Red Ring of Death scenario (which cost MS another cool billion), the boat was undoubtedly pushed out in other elements of the design. Microsoft went to AMD for an advanced graphics core design that featured technology that hit the market before it was even incorporated into PC graphics architecture. Not only that, but both the CPU and GPU were fabricated at 90nm - a production process that was state-of-the-art at the time and nowhere near mature: costly and with low chip yields. Factor in a UK launch price point of just £209 for the base "Core" model and £280 for the hard drive equipped Premium version and the amount of money the platform holder must have been losing per unit was surely eye-watering in the extreme.

To put things into perspective, Sony - launching one year later - was still having problems with the 90nm production process. The Cell processor had to have one its SPUs disabled in order to produce enough viable chips, whereas the RSX graphics core - a late addition to the PS3 spec when it became clear that a second Cell couldn't handle the job - featured a number of cut-backs designed to increase chip yields: the RSX design features 28 ALU (arithmetic logic unit) pipelines, but four are inactive in the final chip. Half of the 16 ROPs (render output units) present in the silicon are disabled. What issues Microsoft had with 90nm remain unknown but there were no known cutbacks in the actual designs. Crucially though, chip yield percentages for the launch period were never revealed - the company may simply have taken the hit, knowing that efficiencies would improve.

> "It was a technological arms race gone mad, the irony being that Nintendo's low-tech Wii came along at a substantially lower price-point and in terms of hardware sales at least, blew both of them away"

Sony splashed the cash in other ways of course. Its Blu-ray drive - apparently the cause of its year-long delay - was extremely expensive at the time, but a key component in the company's attempt to dominate the HD movie market. Construction and finish of the launch PS3 unit was clearly a step above the Xbox 360: the additional complexity in the design was self-evident and the cooling system was clearly light years beyond the Microsoft box. Plus of course, every PlayStation 3 came with a hard drive as standard, and the vast majority of them featured WiFi too. Even with a launch price of £425 in the UK, Sony was still losing money hand over fist.

It was a technological arms race gone mad, the irony being that Nintendo's low-tech Wii came along at a substantially lower price-point and in terms of hardware sales at least, blew both of them away. It's widely believed that Nintendo was in profit on each unit from day one since the internals of the Wii are much the same as the Gamecube's, with a boost to clock speed.

Fast forward to today's era of economic conservatism and it's extremely difficult to imagine that we will see anything like this level of brilliant, breathtaking insanity again. Sony and Microsoft's console businesses are actually profitable now: it's hard to believe that either of them will ever recover the untold billions lost at the beginning of the current gen era and both companies will like the feeling of being solvent again. While we can still expect next-gen consoles to be sold at a loss at launch, it's very unlikely that the designs will be as advanced as they were back in the day and the projected return to profit will happen sooner rather than later.

With the new Wii U, we already have some measure of what Nintendo's plans are. This is a unit that attempts to refresh a current gen HD console design with a revised, more efficient tri-core IBM CPU and an AMD Radeon off-shoot that should be relatively cheap to produce. Mature, established production processes are used to maximise chip yields, while components that have collapsed in price over the years will almost certain offer Nintendo most of its competitive advantages - we should expect to see 1GB or 1.5GB of RAM in there, and a decent amount of flash storage to accommodate its ambitious digital download strategy.

Short of a massive last-minute spec boost, it seems clear that Nintendo is building this machine to a price - and hopefully that will be passed onto the consumer. Even the show-stopping tablet controller is based on cost-efficient parts: its screen is larger than PlayStation Vita's, but runs with a significantly lower resolution. The capacitive multi-touch screen we even see on sub-£100 Android tablets isn't present - instead, a less responsive single-touch resistive display is utilised, hence the inclusion of a DS-esque stylus.

> "The exotic hardware designs championed by Ken Kutaragi have given way to the concept of cramming as much PC power as possible into a console-shaped box - at a price that's right."

As for the next-gen plans of Microsoft and Sony, just the timing of their new launches suggests some caution and an eye towards economy. The Q4 2013 release window being mooted for Durango and Orbis doesn't just give PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 another year to generate decent profits, it also allows for more ambitious designs to be produced more cheaply. The 28nm fabrication process we can expect to see utilised in both consoles is just moving into mainstream production now with the current-gen Radeon and GeForce graphics cards, but the technology is still expensive and chip yields uncertain. By the time we move into 2013 - where both Microsoft and Sony will need to commit to multi-million production runs - the amount of usable chips will be higher, and the costs to produce them lower.

Elsewhere within the designs we should expect to see other mature technologies deployed. Both Durango and Orbis will feature Blu-ray disc drives; they are no longer the exotic technology they were back in 2006 but mass-produced commodities. Memory has also collapsed in price, though whether 512MB GDDR5 RAM modules will be in mass production at a viable price-point in time for a next-gen console launch remains to be seen. In an ideal world, Sony and Microsoft would be looking at eight chips per motherboard for a 4GB capacity, but current volume GDDR5 production remains at 256MB per chip: this may be the area where the platform holders will need to take a hit initially.

Rumours from a number of sources also suggest that economies are also being made elsewhere. Increasingly stronger and more plausible sources are suggesting that Orbis is based on existing PC parts from AMD repurposed into console form. With PlayStation Vita, the post-Kutaragi era Sony went for off-the-shelf parts that offered the most power and performance for the best price-point. Licensing technology isn't cheap, but it's significantly less expensive than creating a brand new processing architecture from scratch - as Sony did with Cell. Other benefits include the ability to tap into AMD's proven expertise in combining CPU and GPU into a single chip (very useful for later console revisions) plus the fact that developers are simply more comfortable with more traditional processor designs.

And what of Durango? By far the most interesting and plausible report on this comes from VG247, and it suggests a fascinating design choice: that the next Microsoft console will actually contain two graphics cores. This may sound like a somewhat exotic, expensive choice but it could make a whole lot of sense. Two slower, narrower chips should be easier to make than one larger one, and in theory it would be significantly cheaper to incorporate two 128-bit memory buses as opposed to one 256-bit interface. Cooling - a key failure in the original Xbox 360 - should also cheaper and easier to handle as heat would be more evenly distributed across the motherboard.

There would be advantages for developers too, as one source told me:

"In the worst case, you could tile, sending half the scene to one GPU and half the scene to the other, losing some efficiency on border-overlapping geometry; a deferred renderer would lose nothing in efficiency in all the lighting and shading passes," we were told.

> "In some ways the lack of exotic hardware is a little disappointing. The grand visions we saw in years gone by have been replaced by a combination of pragmatic realism and economic necessity"

"In the best case, you can parallelise independent operations - for example, rendering the main scene with rendering the shadow map, rendering the different cascades of the increasingly popular cascaded shadow maps, rendering light buffers, rendering different portions of a complex post-processing chain (but post-processing is a good candidate for simple tiling too)."

Way back in 2005, the world was a different place. Sony wanted to re-define computing, replace DVD with Blu-ray HD movies and produce a state-of-the-art games machine. Microsoft wanted a high-end PC in a box, without involving Intel or NVIDIA after unsuccessful collaborations on the original Xbox. To achieve their goals, unimaginable amounts of money were thrown at the problem.

In Microsoft's case it spent a fortune to achieve a year's headstart over Sony - but arguably the effort was worth it. It has achieved wonders in breaking Sony's complete domination of the console marketplace, but stumbled in terms of reliability and build quality. For its part, Sony has seen off HD-DVD (though perhaps did not foresee the prominence of streaming movie services) and produced the most technologically advanced games of the era - but the full extent of Ken Kutaragi's vision for the Cell processor never came to be, and the PS3 with all its triumphs and shortfalls proved to the last console produced under his stewardship.

In some ways the lack of exotic hardware being mooted for the next-gen consoles is a little disappointing. The grand visions we saw - particularly from Sony - have been replaced by a combination of pragmatic realism and economic necessity: both of these machines will almost certainly be PC tech repurposed into games consoles. The challenge for Microsoft and Sony will be to produce a generational leap that matters to a mainstream audience at a price that works: £299, anyone?

Random: Xbox Fan Shares Clip Of Microsoft's Console Factory Line From 2006

We miss you, Xbox 360

Look, we're not out here to ruin anyone's day or anything, but the Xbox 360 is officially 20 years old this year. You read that right, November 2025 marks two whole decades since Microsoft's seminal Xbox console first launched - which is a bit of a scary thought, if we're honest. However, we do have lots of nostalgia for that period, and an old video clip has resurfaced that transports us right back to the time of Project Gotham Racing and Gears of War.

Shared on Reddit earlier this week, an old video clip from now-defunct outlet '1Up' depicts an old Xbox 360 manufacturing line from circa 2006. Here, we can see original Xbox 360 models being put together ahead of retailers stocking them on store shelves.

Looking back now, this is such an iconic console design, and no later Xbox 360 model ever captured that same magic, did it? Sure, it felt a bit plasticky to touch and we of course remember the Red Ring of Death fiasco (which we're painfully reminded of in this video), but still - what a console and what times we were living in back then as Xbox fans!

As we close in on that 20-year anniversary, we do hope Microsoft commemorates the Xbox 360 in a big way later this year. It continues to be their most championed era for lots of gamers out there, and after the amazing 2021 celebrations for OG Xbox, we have high hopes for something similar later this year. How about another batch of backwards compatible titles, eh Microsoft?

webpage.text:
WWIII: IGN AU's Next-Gen Console Showdown

Bennett:
The time has come. We've given the latest next-gen console six weeks to settle in to the Australian market. We've had plenty of time to play extensively with the PS3, the Wii and the Xbox 360 (whether we wanted to or not is another question). And now, at last, we're ready. Ready to judge. Ready to tell you, dear reader, whether the Wii, the PS3 or the Xbox 360 is our pick for best overall console. And finally, ready to provoke the flames of several hundred thousand Australians who spent money on one or more of them. Obviously it's not an easy answer, or I'd simply say 360, Patch would say Wii and Cam would say Atari 2600, and the article would be done. But here goes anyway - and remember, please send any and all flame emails to our new, asbestos-lined inbox at wehateign@ign.ru. Cam, want to explain to our readers how this story is going to unfurl?
Cam: Certainly, cos if there's one thing I'm good at, it's the art of furling and unfurling. The basic idea is that we're going to examine each next-gen machine in turn, giving our perspectives on basically every important aspect, then we'll wrap it all up with a full-on head to head, where a winner (*gulp*) will be announced. We've already covered Nintendo's Wii and Sony's PlayStation 3, so the last stop on our next-gen tour is the Magnavox Odyssey. Sorry, the Xbox 360.


The Launch

Cam: The first of the major platform holders to dive headfirst into the next-gen market, Microsoft did a great job with the Xbox 360, and it showed at the launch. Again, the delay on the Australian release meant that by the time our launch rolled around, the game selection had filled out somewhat. It was a well-rounded list, with the likes of DOA 4, GRAW, Oblivion, Amped 3, Top Spin 2, Call of Duty 2, Condemned, Full Auto, Kameo, Perfect Dark Zero, Prey, The Outfit and PGR 3 in the roster. Perhaps no truly killer apps, but a strong selection nonetheless. The launch was met with plenty of enthusiasm too, with crowded midnight launches around the country. The result? The 360 shifted over 30,000 units in its first four days on sale in Australia with a decent initial attach rate of 2.6 games per machine.


I guess the biggest downside of the arrival of the 360 - both in Australia and overseas, was how swiftly it brought the original Xbox to an end. The system didn't really see a full console cycle on the market, and by the time the 360 was on the horizon, plenty of publishers essentially dropped their support. In a lot of ways the Xbox was a very expensive experiment for Microsoft, and that left quite a few gamers high and dry. Moving on was probably the best thing for the company to do though - Xbox was never going to get the mainstream traction PS2 has. The upshot, however, is that Sony is in a fantastic position to capitalise on the strength of its brand - it can support both its console systems simultaneously and gradually move PS2 owners onto PS3. Thoughts on the launch Mr Kolan?

Patch: My thoughts, eh? Microsoft nailed the PAL launch, even if the North American one was plagued by hardware problems and stock shortages and the Japanese 360 was very nearly stillborn. By the time the 360 was birthed in Australia, we had a raft of sweet games that made plonking down AU$650 worthwhile. Specifically, Ghost Recon Advanced Warfighter, Fight Night Round 3 and Oblivion were all available from launch, and for curious Rare fanboys who perhaps jumped ship from Nintendo, Kameo and Perfect Dark Zero were plastered across every surface. The reception in Sydney was loud and chaotic, despite the rain - there were hundreds of people lining up for the midnight countdown, and this is something that not even gaming power-hitter Sony could replicate almost exactly a year later. It was a very strong launch for the 360.


Bennett: Have to agree with you guys - seeing 700 cheering gamers standing in Sydney's pouring rain at midnight was testimony to the warm reception 360 got at launch. Though, given that 360 was first out of the next-gen gate, it would have been hard to fail. The price was nice as well, although I think that releasing a crippled version without a hard drive was a bad move. It's now biting the company in the butt, with the recent outburst from Rockstar and how it's hurting GTA IV development.

The other major issue was reliability, especially in the hot Australian environment. Even though our launch was delayed, the hardware still hadn't been fixed - I don't know of a single 360 owner who still has their original launch 360. Regardless of these problems, the 360 launch couldn't be regarded as anything less than a shiny success story for Microsoft.


The Hardware

Cam: In terms of the hardware, it seems like everyone wins with 360. Gamers get true next-gen horsepower that can single-handedly justify purchase of that gorgeous new HDTV, while the hardware architecture itself is straightforward and familiar for developers. Importantly, plenty of developers have also praised Microsoft's level of support. There's one major issue I have with the hardware, however, and it's one that Bennett just touched on - the lack of a hard drive as standard. That's a baffling decision and one that looks especially misguided in hindsight, given how few gamers have actually picked up the Core system. How long is it going to be until we start seeing games with an "HDD Models Only" sticker on the box? Oh, and I'm also not a fan of the massive external power supply. We used to joke about needing a team of workers fresh from building the pyramids in egypt to lug the original Xbox around, but when you factor in the power supply, the 360 isn't that much smaller. Thankfully you can tuck it away, and the overall aesthetic is much nicer.

Patch: In terms of raw horsepower, games like Gears of War show better than most what the system can crank out when pushed. From an aesthetic standpoint though, I must admit I think the 360 is kind of bland. It's not PS3-grill ugly, but it isn't svelte like Wii either. I think making the sides concave, while kind of trendy, isn't the most practical shape for a console - which by rights should be stackable. That said, the controller is just about the best ever - the stick and button placement, trigger resistance and ergonomic shape is spot-on. Event the heft is just right - not too light, like the PS3, and traditional enough to make the Wii's nunchuck/remote combo look alien. A lack of HD-DVD playback built into the system seems short-sighted, however. Microsoft really should've backed this format properly, rather than letting buyers decide. On one hand, it's amicable. On the other, they need to take the lead sometimes, like Sony has done. It might cost the 360 in the long-term.


Bennett: I think the move to omit HD-DVD was a clever one. Look at the Blu-ray backlash PS3 is getting - gamers prefer choice. If Blu-ray wins the format war, there's nothing to stop Microsoft from releasing an add-on Blu-ray drive.

As far as the guts of the system, we've all seen what the 360 can do when caressed by talented developers. It might have come out a year earlier than PS3, but from a pure hardware perspective, many folks claim the two systems are neck and neck.

Patch is totally spot on regarding the controller. My hands have never been as happy as when they're wrapped around the sheer perfection that is the 360 controller. And who'd have thought that going wireless would make such a difference? If only the thing didn't sound like a jet engine taking off, and was more reliable than the Sydney train service, the 360's hardware would be impossible to fault. Thankfully the new revision due sometime soon, with its shrunken CPU, should fix these issues.

The Current Games Line-up

Cam: Which next-gen console do you guys play most? I'm willing to bet (and not just because we talk about this all the time) that if you added up the hours you spent on Wii and PS3, they'd still pale next to the time spent on 360. That's largely down to two things - the games and the degree of seamless online integration in every title. Even during a game drought (and let's face it, the only truly great 360 games released in the last couple of months are Guitar Hero II and GRAW 2), the back catalogue is strong enough that you'll invariably have something to play, whether online or off. Factor in the release of map packs for games like Gears of War, demos and steady Live Arcade releases and there's generally something happening in the world of 360 to check out.

Patch: I play my DS the most, to be honest. Does that count? No? Fine. 360 is a close second anyway, followed a good hike back by Wii. That says a lot. We go where the gaming is good, and right now, that is on the 360. Things started off a little slow, but the floodgates have since opened and, provided you can tolerate the umpteenth sports and racing title, there is a lot to play right now. I agree with you though, Cam, that the 360 would really be in a more dire position without fresh content updates via the Marketplace. Guitar Hero II's DLC is a tad disappointing, though. Really, if you don't have a net connection, the 360 is kind of like the old gaming hermit on the hill, who only comes down for a session of Gears or Rainbow Six Vegas.


Bennett: The stack of quality 360 titles on my shelf just keeps getting bigger and bigger. For a gamer with my tastes, favouring shooters, driving and action games, the 360 is the perfect platform. These genres are absolutely littered with games that must be played - I'm planning on taking a week's holiday just to get through some of them. It's only going to get better - the 360 has easily the most impressive list of upcoming games. Halo 3, Alan Wake, DiRT, Forza 2, RE5, GTAIV, etc, etc. I think I might extend that one week holiday into two…

But the line-up isn't perfect. I don't know why, but Microsoft doesn't seem to get mainstream games. They've tried, with the likes of Kameo and Viva Pi¿ata both bombing badly. Even though Guitar Hero II isn't a first party title, hopefully it'll be the start of a new era of mass gaming for the 360. It needs it - because without mass appeal, the 360 is going to remain a niche hardcore gamer's machine. Which is not a good thing for the future of the platform.


The Services

Cam: Way to jump ahead two topics Bennett. Geez. You don't see me jumping a hundred features ahead to talk about the next Xbox… which, by the way, will come with an anti-gravity pump (for weightless full body gesture controls), a brainstem connection (just don't use one of the dodgy third party brainstem peripherals - you like the feeling in your legs right?) and will be called either "Xbox 24/7" or "Xbox Next: No They Di'int!".

So. Services. Microsoft did a whole lot right in this area. The company made a raft of features compulsory standards, such as Live integration, custom playlists and achievements. A smart move in terms of consistency, but also a stroke of genius in other ways - the most prominent being achievements. It's great to see the old high score ethos back in the modern era. The centralised online approach may have drawbacks (which I'll let Bennett cover in a minute) but it does make the process of playing online and staying up to date simple. Other services have been a bit patchy - Live Arcade had an absolutely rubbish selection for a long time, although it's gradually getting there now (although more quality control wouldn't go astray), while the Australian Marketplace tends to be a bit patchy. Speaking of "Patchy"…

Patch: Ahem. I do love getting serviced by my 360. Xbox Live's Marketplace is easy to use, varied in content and gosh darn it, they keep the sucker updated with fresh local and international content. It's love. Then there is the Media Centre component, the friends list and holy crap - the achievements. If ever there was a feature that had the potential to make me want to play through a crappy game, it is this. In fact, for introducing achievement points into the mix, it adds a whole new competitive dimension that no other platform comes close to offering. It's clever stuff. USB connectivity is something the PS3 does too, so I can't give it full credit. But then again, it's arguable that Sony only went all-out with card readers and similar in vain retaliation to the 360's connectivity, so …full credit? Regardless, I love Live, Marketplace and fresh content.


Bennett: The 360 wouldn't be the experience it is without the cornerstone of Xbox Live. This console was built from the ground up to be a connected device, and it shows. For the most part, it's a polished, easy to use service - provided you can around those nasty NAT issues. The in-game integration is seamless, the Gamertag/friend system is pure simplicity, and forcing every game to use voice makes 360 gaming a rowdy, hilarious affair. Marketplace has evolved into an elegant model of the future of online distribution, and our US friends are blessed with wads of HD content (coming to an Oceanic country near you soon!).

But as the one guy in the office who's spent more than a few (thousand) hours playing over Xbox Live, Cam's right - I'm going to have a little whinge. The lag and connectivity issues for Aussies are a real thorn in the side of the online experience. For every smooth game played with Aussies, local Xbox Live players will have two laggy matches with Germans and Scandinavians. The matchmaking system needs some serious work for smaller regions.

Not many people have seen it, but hooking the 360 up to a PC equipped with HDTV tuners and Windows Media Centre is a fantastic experience. Without fail, every person who's seen it at my home has asked if I could set it up for them. Hopefully this feature will become more commonly used as Vista rolls out into homes.

The Potential

Cam: What does the future hold for Xbox 360? Well, as Bennett mentioned earlier, the system is a haven for hardcore gamers, but can Microsoft expand the audience? Or - better still - can the number of more dedicated gamers keep growing so that the system can continue to do what it does best, while still enjoying massive commercial success? We don't know, but in terms of wooing more casual players, titles like Guitar Hero II certainly help, but Microsoft's efforts to make the 360 more of a family machine have fallen flat on their face up until this point. Rare's excellent Viva Pi¿ata was sadly overlooked by many, while no parent in their right mind is going to buy a 360 over a PS2 for their kid based on the port-alicious licensed kids titles on the system. Nor is anyone going to buy a 360 for the many crappy casual games on Live Arcade that they could easily play on their PC. Then there's Live Anywhere, which brings interoperability between PC, 360 and mobile devices - could that expand the market? I don't know, what am I - a mind reader?

The good news right now is that Xbox 360 has the development momentum. Most multiplatform teams are leading with their Xbox 360 version, the games continue to look better, and there's a huge line-up of killer games on the way. The 360 has also led the way in terms of online play and online functionality, and will continue to do so.


Patch: That's a mighty summary right there - in fact, there is little to be added, apart from this: Japan. The potential in Japan is huge, particularly if the PS3 doesn't get the market penetration that it needs to make expensive epic games a worthwhile endeavour. What I am saying is, we might well see an even greater shift by Japanese developers towards making content for 360 in the coming years - multiplatform and exclusive, retail and Marketplace. Also, I'm going to go out on a limb and say that Metal Gear Solid 4 will definitely make its way to the Xbox 360 in some form after a set period on PS3. It just will. There is also a lot of potential in online distribution coming up - the US has been a testbed for direct-download entertainment. If and when the Elite comes out in Australia, we might well see an influx of movies and TV in the AU marketplace.

Bennett: To me, and no doubt to Microsoft, the untapped potential for 360 lies in the sea of cash that is mainstream success. It's stitched up the geek crew, now it's time to rope in the mums and dads, girls and children. And there are two barriers to this - the price, and the games. Even with Guitar Hero II on the platform, the software problem is a long way from being solved. But in my not so humble opinion, even more important is pricing.

The number one competitor in terms of mainstream gaming is the PS2, and a big part of its success there is the oh-so-low price of below $200. For the 360 to tap into this market, it needs to realign its price with something that isn't so far off $199. Even a drop to $400, where the Wii happily sells its ass off to gamers and senior citizens alike, would help its cause. Sell enough units, and the gesture-based karaoke games will follow the install base.


The Wrap-Up

Do you agree or disagree with the IGN AU crew? Is steam literally venting from your ears, or are you nodding your head in silent agreement? Whatever the case, stay tuned for our conclusion, to see which next-gen console gets the nod from us. You can also check out our analysis of the Wii and the PlayStation 3.

metadata.description: The time has come. We've given the latest next-gen console six weeks to settle in to the Australian market. We've had plenty of time to play extensively with the PS3, the Wii and the Xbox 360 (whether we wanted to or not is another question). And now, at last, we're ready. Ready to judge. Ready to tell you, dear reader, whether the Wii, the PS3 or the Xbox 360 is our pick for best overall console.

resultats_lens.texte_contexte: IGN AU examines the next-gen console market in Australia after six weeks, comparing the PS3, Wii, and Xbox 360. Microsoft's Xbox 360 launch in Australia featured a game selection including DOA 4, GRAW, Oblivion, Amped 3, Top Spin 2, Call of Duty 2, Condemned, Full Auto, Kameo, Perfect Dark Zero, Prey, The Outfit, and PGR 3. The console shifted over 30,000 units in its first four days on sale in Australia, bringing the original Xbox cycle to an end.
